newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada pension fund could roil markets.
newsitem.headline: Canada pension fund could roil markets.

text.p: A plan to allow Canada's federal government pension plan to invest in stocks and bonds could rock Canadian financial markets if the government fails to lift its restrictions on foreign investment.
The proposed reform, which is designed to improve the funding of Canada's pension plan (CPP) by boosting premiums 70 percent, will create a huge investment fund with discretionary investment powers.

"You can't have that kind of money flow coming into a market with somewhat limited supply without having some kind of effect," said Fred Ketchen, director of equity trading at the Toronto-based brokerage ScotiaMcLeod.
The impact of the proposal, which is almost certain to become law, will be watched closely by the U.S. government, which is considering a similar restructuring of its Social Security system.

The CPP fund will initially have C$35 billion ($26 billion) to invest -- C$40 billion ($29 billion) less a C$5 billion ($3.7 billion) float for the payout of current benefits -- growing to C$45 billion ($33 billion) in five years and about C$100 billion ($73 billion) in a decade, Finance Department officials said.
The CPP will rival the Quebec government-owned Caisse de depot et placement du Quebec, now the most powerful investment fund in the country, with assets of about C$51 billion ($37 billion).

Under the reform plan, the CPP fund will be required, like private pension plans, to plunge 80 percent of its cash into domestic investments. CPP funds are currently lent to the provinces at preferred rates of interest.

Forcing this behemoth to keep most of its money in Canada could have dramatic consequences for domestic markets, inflating the prices of blue-chip shares and concentrating large amounts of government bonds in the hands of the CPP fund.
While the swell of cash could cushion the market during a correction, it could destabilise some stocks when a fund of this size adjusted its holdings.
Analysts said prudent, arm's-length management and changes to the foreign ownership restrictions were need to minimise the impact on debt and equity markets.

The fund will be restricted in the first three years of the plan to passive investments in bonds and equity index funds. Afterwards, its 12-member government-appointed board can decide whether to invest directly in the stock market.

Analysts said while it would take a number of years to deploy all the cash in the fund, the CPP fund could ultimately become a major stock market investor with influential holdings in some corporations.
Canadian pension funds such as Ontario Teachers, the Ontario Municipal Employees Retirement System and the Caisse, wield enormous clout in Canadian markets.

"Pension funds, when they buy, are going to provide underlying strength to the market. But pension funds often change their mind about one stock and buy another one. So I think that the volatility could be a little greater than it would be under normal circumstances," Ketchen said.

Since the fund will be eyeing long-term growth rather than swift gains, analysts believe most of the cash will probably be chasing the top 100 blue-chip shares rather than buying broadly in the market.

"With keeping the money in Canada, or at least forcing it to stay in Canada, will you get a skew if so much money is chasing the top 100 vs. the other thousands of stocks that are out there -- never mind other investment ideas like venture capital?" asked Mark Mullins, chief economist at brokerage Midland Walwyn.

Analysts are also concerned about the impact on debt markets of another large buyer, particularly since the Canadian government is on the road to becoming a net saver rather than a net borrower -- reducing supply significantly.
"If you do some quick numbers on the fixed-income side, you can imagine this thing owning anywhere between 5 and 15 percent of outstanding Canadian bonds in the Canadian market," Mullins said.
"That's significant, especially in an environment where the government's actually going the other way and is actually redeeming paper," he added.
Mullins said the worst-case scenario for such an inflation of debt prices was a Canadian version of Japan's "bubble economy" of the 1980s, where a spending spree created huge overcapacity.
Investment in the broader market will allow the fund to increase its returns and may ultimately reduce contributions or allow for bigger benefits.
Finance Minister Paul Martin told Reuters that future Canadian governments would probably reduce CPP premiums if the funds invested in stocks performed better than expected.
